newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia's oil group INA signs $150 mln loan.
newsitem.headline: Croatia's oil group INA signs $150 mln loan.

text.p: Croatian state oil group Industrija Nafte d.d. (INA) signed a five-year loan facility on Wednesday worth $150 million with a syndicate of Western banks led by Bankers Trust International (BTI).

The loan, designed for financial and technological restructuring of the largest Croatian company, was priced at 0.875 percent over Libor and will be repayed in one tranche at the end of the period, bankers said.

"The transaction marks the first ever syndication for a Croatian industrial company and the first time any institution other than the Republic of Croatia has obtained financing with a maturity of five years," BTI said in a statement.
Some 21 banks were included in the deal, co-ordinated by BTI and co-arrangers Bank Austria, Dresdner Bank Luxembourg S.A. and Union Bank of Switzerland.
There were no formal government guarantees for the loan.

"The market's overwhelmingly positive reception to this offering is a testimony to the high calibre of INA's management and their well-conceived and executed strategy for restructuring the company," said Stephen O'Neal, Vice President of BTI's Emerging Europe, Middle East and Africa Merchant Bank.

"This transaction will create momentum to enhance future borrowing of both INA and other Croatian companies at significantly lower interest rate levels," O'Neal told Reuters after the signing ceremony at INA headquarters in Zagreb.
The company's new chief executive, former Economy Minister Davor Stern, said INA would meet its commitments.
The bulk of the money -- some $50 million -- will be used to refinance costly liabilities, which alone should save the company several million dollars per year, Stern said.
The rest will be used for technological restructuring, including upgrading the Rijeka refinery and investing in a network of petrol stations across Croatia.
"The loan will enable us to develop INA into a modern, European oil company and prepare it for facing competition which will inevitably come," Stern said.
The company, which accounts for some 10 percent of Croatia's gross domestic product, said earlier it planned to list on the London Stock Exhange by the end of 1999.
It expects to post a pre-tax profit of some 250 million kuna ($40 million) in 1996, after recording a 1.2 billion kuna loss in 1995.

"INA is one of the strongest companies in the region," said Robin Menzel, a senior associate at BTI. "Its input dependency is relatively low, its management is superb and the restructuring was very successful."
INA produces domestically 30 percent of oil and 80 percent of gas needed for production, Menzel said. It controls more than 75 percent of the domestic retail market.

The company was partly restructured when the government took over its considerable foreign liabilities dating back to former Yugoslavia, in a move parallel with the overhaul of its main creditor Privredna Banka.
In exhange the group handed over holdings in some of its non-core businesses and shed other subsidiaries.
It is also seen as having a good chance of expanding into neighbouring eastern European markets including Bulgaria, Romania and Bosnia-Herzegovina, Menzel said.
